---
title: "Virtual Memory — Why One Address Can Mean Different RAM"
description: "A rigorous introductory lesson with one small example, mathematical notation and a proof-oriented explanation."
---

## Start with an ordinary situation

Two programs both access virtual address 0x1000. Why do they not necessarily read the same physical memory?

## The core concept

An operating system gives processes virtual address spaces. Page tables translate virtual page numbers into physical frames and enforce access protections.

## Express it mathematically

$$
a=v\,p+o,\qquad f=M(v),\qquad a_{\rm phys}=f\,p+o
$$

**Every symbol explained:** a is the virtual byte address; p is page size; v is the virtual page number; o is offset within that page; M is a page-table mapping; f is the physical frame number; a_phys is the resulting physical address.

**Substitute actual numbers:** For page size p=4096 bytes and address a=8197, v=2 and o=5 because 8197=2×4096+5. If this process maps virtual page 2 to physical frame 7, the physical address is 7×4096+5=28677. A second process may map its virtual page 2 to frame 12 instead.

## Why it works

Page translation preserves the offset while changing the page number into a frame number. A TLB caches translations; page faults occur if a translation is missing or access needs OS handling. Demand paging does not mean every virtual page always occupies physical RAM.

## Go one level deeper

Actual systems support multiple page sizes, huge pages, shared mappings, copy-on-write, swapped pages, permissions and multiple levels of page tables.

## Common misunderstanding

Virtual address and physical address are different concepts. Never treat pointers printed by two different processes as raw physical locations.

## Check your understanding

Explain the example with different numbers. Identify which assumption makes the derivation work, and which assumption would invalidate it. Then write the mathematical model again without looking.
